nameStory: The name 'scud' comes from the way these tiny crustaceans seem to 'scud' or dart quickly through the water when disturbed. The scientific name 'mucronatus' means 'pointed' in Latin, referring to the sharp spines and pointed features on this little amphipod's body.
description: The Pointed Scud is a tiny shrimp-like crustacean that swims and crawls along the bottom of coastal waters. These translucent creatures are usually less than an inch long, with flattened, curved bodies that look a bit like miniature question marks when they swim. They have long antennae, multiple pairs of legs, and swim on their sides in a distinctive jerky motion. You'll often find them in large numbers scuttling around in shallow tide pools or under rocks.

idTips.label: Body shape and swimming
idTips.description: Swims on its side in a distinctive comma or question-mark shape, darting through water with jerky, rapid movements that stop and start suddenly

idTips.label: Size and color
idTips.description: Tiny translucent body usually less than 3/4 inch long, often with a slightly greenish or grayish tint that makes them blend with seaweed

idTips.label: Pointed features
idTips.description: Body segments have small sharp spines and pointed projections that you can feel if you gently pick one up - they feel slightly prickly

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of long, thread-like antennae that are constantly moving and twitching as they explore their surroundings

idTips.label: Legs and movement
idTips.description: Multiple pairs of legs that paddle rapidly when swimming but also grip and crawl when moving over surfaces

idTips.label: Group behavior
idTips.description: Often found in large numbers together, creating a writhing mass of tiny bodies when you lift a rock or disturb seaweed

habitat: Look for Pointed Scuds in shallow coastal waters along New England's rocky shores and salt marshes. They thrive in tide pools, under rocks, among seaweed, and in the spaces between barnacles and mussels where the water stays cool and moist. You'll find the highest numbers in areas with good water circulation and plenty of decaying organic matter to feed on.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm up, often found in large congregations under rocks and in shallow pools during low tide.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're easiest to spot darting around tide pools and among seaweed during daylight hours.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may move to slightly deeper water or more protected areas as temperatures begin to drop.
seasonality.winter: Less active and harder to find, typically hiding deep under rocks and in crevices where water temperature stays more stable.

funFact: These tiny scuds are actually ecosystem engineers - they can completely change the chemistry of tide pools by processing enormous amounts of decaying seaweed and other organic matter, with a single scud capable of eating half its body weight in dead material every single day!
confusionNotes: Often confused with tiny shrimp or even water fleas, but scuds swim on their sides while shrimp swim upright, and scuds are much more compressed (flattened) from side to side. Remember: 'Scuds swim sideways, shrimp swim straight up.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'scuds,' these aren't insects at all - they're crustaceans more closely related to lobsters and crabs than to any bug. The term 'amphipod' means 'different feet' because they have several different types of legs for different purposes - some for swimming, others for gripping, and others for feeding.
compareHints: Pointed Scuds are distinguished from their cousin the Tide-pool Scud by their more prominent spines and pointed body segments that give them their name. While Tide-pool Scuds tend to be smoother and more rounded, Pointed Scuds have a distinctly 'spiky' feel when handled gently. Both species often live in the same tide pools, but Pointed Scuds prefer areas with more wave action and stronger currents.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Gammarus fasciatus is distinguished from its saltwater cousin the Tide-pool Scud by its smaller size and freshwater habitat, while Gammarus mucronatus tends to be slightly larger and more robust.
Tide-pool scuds differ from their freshwater cousin, the common scud (Gammarus fasciatus), by their tolerance for salt water and slightly more robust build.
